newsitem.title: UK: P&O Nedlloyd leaves shipping alliances in flux.
newsitem.headline: P&O Nedlloyd leaves shipping alliances in flux.

text.p: Membership of the two largest container shipping alliances remains fluid despite Anglo-Dutch shipping group P&O Nedlloyd's announcement on Tuesday to join the Grand Alliance.

The make-up of the Grand and Global alliances was thrown open earlier this year by the merger of P&O Containers and Nedlloyd's container shipping operations and by plans announced by Singapore's Neptune Orient Lines Ltd (NOL) to take over APL Ltd of the U.S. for $825 million.
Both new pairings brought together companies in rival alliances.

Container shipping alliances allow companies to share the heavy investment costs of building sufficiently large fleets to operate on long haul routes calling at all major ports with regular scheduled services. They can also help cut container positioning and terminal use costs.
Loss of a major partner from an alliance could undermine their ability to operate the same number and regularity of services and port calls.
The Grand Alliance had comprised NOL, Hapag-Lloyd AG of Germany, Japan's Nippon Yusen Kaisha and P&O Containers, part of Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co of the UK.

The Global Alliance linked APL with Japan's Mitsui OSK Lines, Nedlloyd Groep NV, Malaysian International Shipping Corp Bhd, and Hong Kong's Orient Overseas Container Lines (OOCL) which is part of Orient Overseas (International) Ltd ).
Speculation among shipping analysts has long suggested that Nedlloyd would join the Grand Alliance and NOL move to the Global Alliance. Nedlloyd has now completed the first step.
P&O Nedlloyd said Tuesday it has alternative plans to replace NOL if the Singapore group switches to the Global Alliance to be with APL.
P&O Nedlloyd corporate communications manager Daniel Sikkens told Reuters: "The NOL-APL merger has no bearing on our decision. We would welcome NOL to stay but have alternatives to hand if they go."
However, it is also possible that NOL could take APL to the Grand Alliance leaving the Global Alliance badly weakened.
A spokesman for NOL in London said the Singapore-based carrier had not yet announced any decision on its plans.
Global Alliance member OOCL said in a statement today that the P&O Nedlloyd decision would allow for an orderly redeployment of the two groupings fleets from early 1998.
OOCL said: "The details of next year's deployment are still being discussed and the future long-term service structure will be announced in due course."
"During the interim period until phase out of Nedlloyd's vessels, the Global Alliance network will not be impacted," the Hong Kong-based carrier added.
OOCL, which has a container slot sharing agreement with APL, said the Global Alliance would continue to build on long term plans to expand its services.

Sikkens said P&O Nedlloyd's decision was based on a combination of three strategic aims - to maintain its leading position in the Far-East to Europe and Atlantic trades while growing in the Pacific, the best utilisation of assets and the lowest costs.
He cited P&O Nedlloyd's plans to build four 2,900 teu ships while NYK was building five 5,800 teu vessels as an example of asset synergies.

But if NOL quit the Grand Alliance, shipping analysts speculate that the alliance's need to strengthen its position on the U.S. west coast might require the group to attract one of the remaining Global Alliance members, such as OOCL or MISC, or an independent line - possibly a South Korean shipping group. -Paul Berrill Reuters Shipping News + 44 171 542 4087.
